claims.text: Thermogravimetric analysis can be used to assess high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Thermogravimetric analysis can be used to assess phase stability.
TGA detects mass gains associated with oxygen uptake.
Changes in the rate of mass gain can signal underlying phase transformations.
Heating the material in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere can cause formation and growth of a surface oxide scale.
Structural phase changes may occur within the material during high-temperature oxidation testing.
High-temperature oxidation leads to oxygen uptake.
Oxygen uptake causes an increase in specimen mass.
Inflection points or other variations in a mass-gain curve may indicate phase transformations.
Phase transformations can alter oxidation kinetics or material structure.
Under oxygen-rich heating between approximately 900°C and 1200°C, the TGA curve will show a gradual mass increase.
The TGA curve will exhibit distinct slope changes at temperatures where oxidation or phase transitions occur.
The same material heated under nitrogen or argon should show negligible mass change in the absence of oxidation.
TGA may be ineffective when oxidation is too slow to produce a detectable mass change.
TGA may be ineffective for phase transitions that do not significantly alter oxidative behavior.
TGA mass changes cannot necessarily be attributed directly to specific phase transitions without complementary in situ structural analysis.
High-temperature XRD can independently track phase changes during the proposed experiment.
Similar TGA behavior in oxidizing and inert atmospheres would falsify the claim that TGA reliably reflects oxidation behavior and phase stability in this test.
